title: Solidarity
hook: John Paul II's visits home to Poland and a peaceful workers' movement that changed the country

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Paul the Second, the pope from Poland. Your line was be not afraid.

A gate at a shipyard on the Baltic coast of Poland. The workers inside are on strike, locked in. On the gate hang flowers, a picture of the Virgin Mary, and a photograph of the Polish pope. Outside, families pass food through the bars. Inside, a priest hears confessions in the open yard, and the strikers kneel on the concrete for Mass. The strike leader is an electrician with a big mustache named Lech Wałęsa. The movement being born on that dock will be called Solidarity.
screen: `A SHIPYARD GATE ON THE BALTIC.` → `FLOWERS, MARY, THE POPE.` → `MASS ON THE CONCRETE.`

segments.voice: First, the visit. Not long after he became pope, John Paul went home to Poland, then under a communist government. Enormous crowds came out. In Warsaw he prayed aloud that the Spirit would come down and renew the face of the earth, and then added: the face of this land. He was borrowing a psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "thou shalt renew the face of the earth." Some who were there say people looked around and realized how many of them there were. Second, the strike. At the shipyard in Gdańsk, workers struck, and out of the strikes came Solidarity, a trade union the government didn't control. Its badge became the word itself, painted in tumbling red letters. Third, the hard years. The government declared martial law, banned the union and jailed its leaders. Solidarity went underground. A young Warsaw priest, Jerzy Popiełuszko, held Masses for the country and preached a line from Saint Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "overcome evil by good." The secret police murdered him. His funeral became a sea of people, and still the movement didn't turn to violence. Fourth, the end. The government sat down with Solidarity at a round table and agreed to partly free elections, and Solidarity's candidates swept the seats open to them. Communist rule in Poland ended without a civil war, and some historians link the movement to the wider changes that soon followed across Eastern Europe. Catholic teaching calls solidarity a virtue: a firm commitment to the good of every person, because we are all responsible for all. In Poland, it was also a union card.
screen: `THE POPE GOES HOME.` · `A STRIKE BECOMES A UNION.` · `MARTIAL LAW, A MARTYRED PRIEST.` · `A ROUND TABLE, NOT A WAR.` · then, large: `OVERCOME EVIL BY GOOD.`

segments.voice: Count the people who worked yesterday so your life could run: whoever picked your food, drove the truck, cleaned the building, stocked the shelf. Pick one face and wonder what their shift is like, and what would make it fairer. If you pray, pray for workers with Paul's line, overcome evil by good; if not, hold them with gratitude.
Solidarity. The Polish workers' union born in the Gdańsk shipyard, and a Catholic virtue: a firm commitment to the good of all.
Your line: without violence. The week ran from Vatican II through Paul the Sixth, Romero, the four churchwomen, the Missionaries of Charity and John Paul, to Solidarity. That's the week.

howItsDone: In Gdańsk, a monument to the shipyard workers stands at the gate where the strike began, and Polish Catholics visit the grave of Blessed Jerzy Popiełuszko at his Warsaw parish.

chat.says: How did Solidarity beat a communist government without fighting?
options: It stayed nonviolent, even after a priest's murder, and won partly free elections at a round table.
It didn't; Polish soldiers sided with the strikers and took over the government.
The pope made a secret deal with the government, then announced it from Rome.
chat.meaning: Through martial law and Popiełuszko's murder, Solidarity refused violence; round-table talks brought partly free elections, and communist rule ended without a civil war.
